title-group.article-title: Emerging strategies to enhance microbial natural product–based drug discovery

abstract.p: Natural products (NPs) have served as a major source of chemically novel, bioactive therapeutics for the treatment of various diseases. In recent years, NP discovery has benefited greatly from advancements in biotechnological fields. This review covers techniques and tools from 2022 to 2025 that have expanded NP discovery capabilities through gene-editing tools to activate silent biosynthetic genes, cell-free methods for NP production and diversification, as well as artificial intelligence and informatics tools for structure generation and correlational studies.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Natural products (NPs), or secondary metabolites, are bioactive compounds generated by organisms to gain a competitive advantage in their environment [1]. These potent compounds have been co-opted by humans for millennia due to their therapeutic potential. NPs exhibit a diverse array of bioactivities — including antimicrobial, anti-inflammatory, and anti-cancer, among others — making them a cornerstone of drug discovery. Microorganisms are a premier source of NPs due to their significant taxonomic diversity and biosynthetic complexity [2,3]. An estimated 70% of all current antibacterial agents are of microbial origin, emphasizing their relevance to the pharmaceutical industry [1,2].

Historically, microbial NPs were identified through laborious techniques such as bioactivity-guided fractionation, in which crude organic extracts are subjected to multiple rounds of purification and continuously monitored for a desired activity to eventually yield the responsible compound(s) [3]. While this method has uncovered powerful drugs used in clinics, only a small subset of compounds is accessible by this method. Many NPs are produced in minute quantities or are unstable in laboratory conditions, creating a significant roadblock to their discovery and study [1]. This, among other factors, has contributed to a decreasing number of novel NPs entering clinical trials in recent times [4].

In response, developments from the biotechnological sector offer new methodologies to discover NPs inaccessible by traditional means. For instance, the advent and expansion of genome sequencing led to the development of genome mining, which has now become a standard tool to interrogate candidate NP genes [1,3,4]. Likewise, genetic and microbial engineering have enabled heterologous expression systems to selectively overexpress biosynthetic genes outside their native hosts [3]. These and other strategies have ushered in a new era of microbial NP research that co-evolves with technological advancements. With the tremendous progress being made in this field, the applications of these strategies in microbial NP research warrant further discussion. Thus, this review will focus on recent (2022–2025) developments in enhancing microbial NP discovery (Figure 1). After an overview of each subsection, representative articles will be discussed in further detail.

sec.title: Enhanced strategies for activating cryptic biosynthetic pathways
sec.p: Developments in genomic analysis have accelerated the discovery of silent and cryptic biosynthetic gene clusters (BGCs), which in turn have necessitated the refinement of current genetic manipulation tools. Such tools can be broadly categorized by whether they activate BGCs within the native strain of interest or redesign the BGC for enhanced expression in a heterologous host [5]. For the former, Clustered Regularly Interspaced Short Palindromic Repeats (CRISPR) technologies are often employed, and recent advancements have enabled their use in a wider variety of contexts. In the latter, new refactoring strategies that include genetic, epigenetic, and protein-mediated regulation have expanded the available avenues for gene activation.

sec.title: CRISPR-aided activation of native biosynthetic genes
sec.p: In the thirteen years since its discovery, CRISPR-Cas9 has been readily used to activate silent BGCs owing to its gene-editing capabilities [6]. Recent combinations with other gene-editing tools have expanded the range of bacterial species in which it can be employed [7], and new applications such as BGC capture within the same cell have even been developed [8]. Modifications to Cas9 have increased its efficiency in Streptomyces species [9], though alternative strategies to CRISPR-Cas9, such as phiC31 integration, have been more successful in this ubiquitous and NP-rich genus [5]. One exemplary strategy is the reengineering of a class I CRISPR system for genetic manipulation of non-model Streptomyces strains [10]. Thus, the innovative method developed by Zhou et al. uses a dual-plasmid system to express a modified CRISPR-Cascade complex and scaffold RNA (scRNA). Once the complex is integrated, modular incorporation of any scRNA makes this a flexible and efficient approach for targeted BGC activation (Figure 2a). As these systems are endogenous to many Streptomyces species, the CRISPR-Cascade complex was found to conjugate with greater efficiency than the foreign Cas9 [10].

sec.title: Combinatorial refactoring for multi-enzyme optimization
sec.p: Although an established technique, new technologies and applications have enabled developments in refactoring strategies for gene activation. Targeting the crossover between primary and secondary metabolism has recently emerged as an exciting strategy for refactoring-based overexpression, with recent studies identifying primary metabolites involved in the production of many NPs [11]. Some articles have emphasized epigenetic regulation [12], while others have identified key regulatory proteins that dramatically improve NP production without affecting neighboring genes [13,14]. Xue et al. recently implemented an innovative refactoring and heterologous overexpression strategy to enhance class III lanthipeptide production in Firmicutes (Figure 2b) [15]. Most heterologous overexpression strategies rely on either a replicative plasmid, providing high expression levels to its encoded genes, or an integrative plasmid that confers expression stability. To leverage the benefits of each, Xue et al. cloned lanthipeptide precursor peptide-encoding genes into a replicative plasmid and the corresponding post-translational modification (PTM) enzyme-encoding genes into an integrative plasmid. After adding strong inducible promoters, they expressed both plasmids in a Bacillus subtilis 168 host. This combinatorial strategy enabled the group to subsequently investigate the structure and activity of novel lanthipeptides produced from the refactored BGC, termed paenithopeptins, which bear rare N,N-dimethylations that confer antibacterial activity. The authors also utilized this strategy with another class III lanthipeptide BGC encoding bacinapeptin and observed similar levels of overexpression, indicating its potential for interrogating other lanthipeptide BGCs [15].

sec.title: Strategies for cell-free natural product production and modification
sec.p: Cell-based methods are common across NP discovery but can be hindered by unoptimized host strains or culture conditions. Additionally, the chemical space accessible through these methods is limited by the current scope of known BGCs [1]. Cell-free methods have thus been developed to address these concerns via flexizyme (Fx)-guided de novo peptide synthesis and high-throughput NP functionalization.

sec.title: In vitro transcription and translation of new-to-nature peptides and other natural products
sec.p: Recent improvements to cell-free biosynthesis (CFB) systems have enabled high-throughput NP discovery based on the in vitro transcription-translation (IVT) of DNA templates. Peptides can be easily generated using this method, and the addition of PTM enzymes and Fx, ribozymes that enable tRNAs to be loaded with non-canonical amino acids (ncAAs) [16], multiplies their potential structural diversity. For example, new-to-nature ribosomally synthesized and post-translationally modified peptides (RiPPs) with user-defined features can be designed using computational algorithms and quickly produced with CFB [17]. Artificial intelligence (AI) has also been employed to design novel antimicrobial peptides (AMPs) and thiopeptides [18–20]. Recent studies have expanded the accessible NP chemical space by utilizing the ribosome to generate nonstandard skeletons [21] or introducing PTMs to add diverse functional groups [22]. Apart from the ribosome, nonribosomal peptide synthetases (NRPSs) and polyketide synthases have been successfully expressed in cell-free systems [23,24], opening the door for future investigation of the diverse NPs produced by these complex enzymes. The work of Pelton et al. exemplifies current CFB efforts, as they interrogate the limitations of this technology and improve it through cheminformatics [25] (Figure 3a). They first developed an algorithm to examine the structural and biophysical properties of known peptide NPs and classified them by size, cyclization type, the presence of ncAAs, and other parameters. These data were then used to identify peptide building blocks currently inaccessible by CFB, from which they selected the ncAA piperazate (Piz) for further development. While Piz is only incorporated by NRPSs in cells, Pelton et al. designed Fxs to enable its use by the ribosome in a cell-free system. Their approach not only expanded the accessible chemical space of CFB but also laid the groundwork for future efforts towards the de novo design of ncAA-containing peptide NPs [25].

sec.title: High-throughput natural product modification for analog generation
sec.p: Despite their potency, NPs frequently require modifications to achieve drug-like properties. This time-consuming process makes the development of high-throughput modification platforms a pressing need in the field. RiPPs have emerged as excellent candidates for modification due to the vast array of PTM enzymes associated with their biosynthesis, enabling selective tailoring [26]. These enzymes are often promiscuous, modifying various NPs to generate diverse NP derivatives and chimeras [26,27]. Enzymatic and chemical modifications to polycyclic NPs have also demonstrated potential to produce potent NP derivatives [28]. One intriguing platform for high-throughput analog production was recently developed by Yamamoto et al. to design AMPs via a combinatory ligation strategy (Figure 3b) [29]. They leveraged the structural similarities between compounds targeting MraY, a bacterial transmembrane protein involved in peptidoglycan synthesis, and developed a chemical library as their starting point. The group then split anti-MraY compounds into core and accessory groups before adding reactive motifs to the cleavage sites. The resulting functionalized fragments were then recombined to generate a series of randomized antimicrobial analogs. This flexible platform could be applied to other NPs that feature structural similarities, enabling their use in high-throughput studies (Figure 3b) [29].

sec.title: Computational strategies to predict and characterize natural products
sec.p: Technologies aimed at analyzing and exploiting big data have become an integral part of NP discovery workflows. For this task, AI and informatics remain the tools of choice for their unmatched analytical capabilities and ability to navigate huge datasets [30]. The following sections will focus on technological advancements and workflows that take advantage of AI’s generative capabilities to produce novel structures, process large unannotated chemical datasets, and interface informatics data to connect NPs with human diseases.

sec.title: Expanding chemical space through generative AI
sec.p: AI tools have become an increasingly attractive method to identify bioactive NP-like compounds due to their ability to identify patterns invisible to traditional analytical tools. Machine- and deep learning–based tools using genomic and metabolic data have been applied to discover NPs from huge datasets and interpret data at unprecedented levels [31–38]. Likewise, generative tools can employ these hidden trends to create structures with desirable features. The resulting compounds can then be prioritized and verified for their pharmacological properties [39]. Tay et al. employed a generative AI model with a long short-term memory (LSTM) recurrent neural network (RNN) architecture to generate structures at an unprecedented scale (Figure 4a) [40]. By training the model with 400 000 known NPs from the COCONUT database, it was able to tokenize the structures into building blocks and rebuild them into putative NPs following a similar chemical logic. The model produced a database of over 67 million unique NP-like structures, dwarfing the COCONUT database by 165-fold and even expanding its chemical space [40]. Previous attempts at such a task have yielded limited novelty and scale [39], marking this collection as a key turning point for the next generation of computational NP discovery.

sec.title: Structural annotation of mass spectral datasets to discover novel chemistry
sec.p: Publicly available mass spectrometry (MS) data collected from high-resolution/accurate mass (HRAM) mass spectrometers have prompted the development of numerous software tools for researchers to aid in the discovery of NPs. Two notable machine learning–based tools — COSMIC (Confidence Of Small Molecule IdentifiCations) and MSNovelist — have emerged as complementary approaches for annotation of metabolites from untargeted tandem MS (MS/MS) data. COSMIC utilizes traditional or in silico–generated spectral libraries, in combination with a support vector machine-generated confidence score, to provide high-confidence structural annotation for both reported and unreported structures. This workflow enabled the identification of 12 previously unknown bile acid conjugates from a publicly available mouse fecal metabolomics dataset, demonstrating its significant potential for unknown metabolite discovery [41]. Complementary to COSMIC, MSNovelist uses an encoder–decoder RNN to generate de novo structural annotations based on structural fingerprints from the input spectra, enabling the annotation of metabolites not captured by spectral library matching-based methods [42]. Both COSMIC (as part of CSI:FingerID) and MSNovelist have been integrated into the cheminformatic tool Sirius, which provides a platform for streamlined metabolomics workflows [43] (Figure 4b).

sec.title: Correlating human microbial metabolites to disease states
sec.p: Hundreds of thousands of microbial sequencing projects have been deposited in publicly available databases to drive the discovery of novel NPs. However, predicting their biological roles remains a challenging bottleneck. Given that metabolites produced by human-associated microbes can influence human health, utilizing these relationships may enable the prioritization of human microbial NPs as drug candidates [44–47]. Thus, a novel approach implemented by Older et al. established a strategy correlating the presence of biosynthetic enzymes in human microbes with human disease incidence to discover bioactive microbial NPs (Figure 4c) [48]. Using metagenomic data from the Inflammatory Bowel Disease Multi’omics Database (IBDMDB), the authors identified a negative correlation between inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) and the abundance of three biosynthetic enzymes in human gut microbes that generate sulfonolipids (SoLs), microbial mimics of human endogenous sphingolipids. This relationship strongly suggested that the production of SoLs may be related to the prevention of IBD, prompting Older et al. to subsequently prioritize SoLs for biological investigation. They then confirmed that administering SoLs reduced the severity of IBD symptoms in a mouse model of colitis, demonstrating the value of informatics for establishing disease relevance in NPs. Similar correlative strategies using metabolomics data have been employed to establish connections between human microbial N-acyl lipids and HIV [49], as well as between human microbial aromatic amino acid metabolites and obesity [50]. Overall, these studies demonstrate the value in leveraging big data for bioactive NP discovery.

sec.title: Conclusions
sec.p: Biotechnological developments have enabled the discovery of microbial NPs previously considered inaccessible, even in the post-genomic era. Advances in the activation of cryptic BGCs and CFB allow unprecedented levels of biosynthetic control that can give rise to previously invisible NPs. Concurrently, informatics and AI developments can take advantage of the growing stock of big data to target and predict NPs with high bioactive potential. As these strategies continue to evolve, efforts to develop economical and streamlined iterations of these technologies will enable their wide-spread application and maximize their impacts. Through this review, we hope to spur interest in these burgeoning technologies and their uses in microbial NP research to inspire their further development for future generations.
